content: Savory, scientifically known as Satureja, is a genus of aromatic plants belonging to the family Lamiaceae, which is closely related to rosemary and thyme. There are approximately 30 species within this genus, with Summer Savory (Satureja hortensis) and Winter Savory (Satureja montana) being the most significant in terms of cultivation. Description Species of Satureja are native to warm temperate regions and can be either annual or perennial plants. These plants are typically low-growing herbs or subshrubs, reaching heights of 15 to 50 centimeters. Their leaves measure between 1 and 3 centimeters in length. The flowers, which are arranged in whorls along the stem, range in color from white to pale pink-violet. Ecology and Cultivation Satureja species serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, which include butterflies and moths. For instance, the caterpillars of the moth Coleophora bifrondella feed exclusively on Winter Savory (Satureja montana). While savory can be cultivated purely for ornamental purposes, plants in this genus require full sun exposure and well-drained soil to thrive. Uses Both Summer Savory and Winter Savory are widely used as culinary herbs to enhance the flavor of food. Summer Savory, preferred by many chefs, is an annual plant and is only available during the summer months. In contrast, Winter Savory is an evergreen perennial, making it available year-round. Savory is a key ingredient in Italian cuisine, particularly in dishes involving beans. It is also used to season the traditional Acadian stew known as fricot. Additionally, Satureja douglasii, commonly referred to as Yerba Buena (Spanish for good herb), is used to prepare herbal tea in the western United States. Winter Savory is also reputed to alleviate flatulence.
